register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Charlestown, Nevis: the birth without a marriage
stops.date_confidence: The year is genuinely disputed and is not settled here. A St. Croix probate document of 1768 gives his age as 13, which most modern scholars read as 1755; Hamilton himself claimed 1757 and never corrected it. The day, 11 January, is the traditional one. Coordinates are the birthplace site, now the Museum of Nevis History.
stops.campa: Rachel Faucette Lavien is still legally the wife of Johann Lavien when she bears a second son to the Scottish factor James Hamilton in a house at Charlestown, on a sugar island of the British Leewards. The child has no legitimate standing and no parish will record him properly. A probate clerk in St. Croix will put his age at thirteen in 1768, which makes this the year; Hamilton will say 1757 and never correct it. He grows up in the cane, on a sugar island where most of the people are enslaved.
stops.quote: all, Puppets danced upon the Wires of a Bastard Bratt of a Scotch Pedlar.
stops.quote_source: John Adams to John Quincy Adams, 20 May 1816, on Hamilton
suggested_refs: The Museum of Nevis History at Charlestown, built on the birthplace site
The 1768 St. Croix probate inventory giving his age as 13
sources: Library of Congress, Alexander Hamilton Papers timeline

stops.name: Christiansted, St. Croix: the father walks out
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the pool, which dated the abandonment 1765. James Hamilton brought the family to St. Croix in 1765 and left in 1766; Chernow ch. 2 and Discovering Hamilton separate the two events by about a year. Month and day are not attested and default to 01.
stops.campa: The family crosses to the Danish island the year before, four of them, James Hamilton carrying debts he cannot pay and Rachel a marriage she cannot dissolve. Within a year the father is gone. Whether he goes because the money runs out or because his leaving spares Rachel a bigamy charge, no document says, and biographers have offered both for two centuries without either winning. Alexander is about eleven. He will write to his father for the rest of his life and receive very little back.
suggested_refs: The Christiansted waterfront and Fort Christiansvaern, Danish West Indies

stops.name: Christiansted, the counting house of Beekman and Cruger
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the pool, which put the clerkship after his mother's February 1768 death. The earliest known Hamilton documents are witness signatures on Beekman and Cruger legal papers of April and August 1767. The clerkship runs c. 1767 to 1772; the pool's 1771-1772 range covers only the five months he ran the house alone. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: A boy of about twelve begins signing his name as witness on the legal papers of the trading house of Beekman and Cruger, on the Christiansted waterfront. The earliest surviving Hamilton documents are these signatures, from April and August, and they are the first proof that he exists at all. The work is cargo manifests, bills of exchange, prices of flour and mules and slaves, the rate of the Danish rigsdaler against the Spanish dollar. In 1771 Cruger leaves the island for months and the boy runs the house alone at sixteen, writing to ship captains in the tone of an owner.
suggested_refs: The surviving Beekman and Cruger letterbook
The 1767 witness signatures, earliest Hamilton documents extant
sources: Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia, Alexander Hamilton

stops.name: Christiansted, the fever in the shared room
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. The disease is not: the pool said yellow fever, and the correction is that contemporary accounts and the probate documents describe only a violent fever taking mother and son together. No name is given here because the record gives none.
stops.campa: A violent fever takes the mother and the son together, in the same room, in the same week. The probate papers and the contemporary accounts name no disease; the yellow fever supplied by later tellers is not in the record. Alexander recovers. Rachel dies on the nineteenth of February, and the court seizes her estate for the benefit of the legitimate son of the Lavien marriage, so that the two boys she raised inherit nothing at all, not even the books. The orphan is thirteen and has an employer but no family.
suggested_refs: The St. Croix probate record of Rachel Faucette Lavien, February 1768
sources: Library of Congress, Alexander Hamilton Papers timeline
Chernow, Alexander Hamilton ch. 2, citing the probate records

stops.name: St. Croix, the letter about the hurricane
stops.date_confidence: The verified pool gives the year 1772 and no month or day for either the storm or the printing. Month and day therefore default to 01. Widely repeated dates for the storm and the Royal Danish American Gazette printing were not in the pool and are not asserted.
stops.campa: A hurricane comes over the island and flattens what it reaches. The clerk writes an account of it, addressed to his absent father, and the Royal Danish American Gazette prints it. The prose is that of a boy who has read the Old Testament and Pope and very little else, and the island reads it and understands that the merchants' clerk is something other than a merchants' clerk. A subscription is raised among the local men of property to send him to the mainland for an education. He never sees St. Croix again.
suggested_refs: The Royal Danish American Gazette printing of the hurricane letter, St. Croix, 1772

stops.name: Boston, the landing at Long Wharf
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 42.3601, -71.0589, which is the centroid of downtown Boston rather than the harbour it was labelled. The colonial landing waterfront is Long Wharf, c. 42.3590, -71.0500.
stops.campa: The ship comes into Boston in October carrying a passenger with a letter of introduction and the manuscript that paid for his berth. The town he steps into is two years past the shooting in King Street and a year short of the tea. He does not stay; he is bound for New Jersey and a grammar school, because he has no Latin and cannot enter a college without it. The money in his pocket is a subscription raised by St. Croix merchants, and it is meant to last him until a degree.
suggested_refs: Long Wharf, Boston, the colonial landing stage
sources: Library of Congress, Alexander Hamilton Papers timeline

stops.name: Elizabethtown, Francis Barber's academy
stops.date_confidence: The pool dates the Elizabethtown period only as late 1772 into 1773. Month is approximated to the arrival and day defaults to 01; neither is attested.
stops.campa: He boards with the Boudinots and the Stevenses and takes Latin, Greek, mathematics and the classics at Francis Barber's academy, working through a curriculum meant for boys of twelve at an age when other students are finishing. Elizabethtown is a Presbyterian town of lawyers and merchants with opinions about Parliament, and the households that feed him are households of men who will sit in the Continental Congress. He has been in the country a month, and the credit he is boarded and tutored on is one letter about a storm.
suggested_refs: Francis Barber's academy at Elizabethtown, New Jersey
The Boudinot house, Elizabeth
sources: Library of Congress, Alexander Hamilton Papers timeline

stops.name: King's College, the pamphlets of a student
stops.date_confidence: Year attested for the enrolment; month and day default to 01. The pamphlet material folded into this stop is attested to 1774 with no month in the pool. Coordinates are the Park Place campus.
stops.campa: Turned down by Princeton, which will not let him accelerate, he enters King's College in New York, an Anglican and loyalist foundation on Park Place. He studies where the college wants and writes where it does not. Answering Samuel Seabury's Westchester Farmer pamphlets, he publishes A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress anonymously, and readers take the author for a mature man. He drills with a volunteer company on the college green. The war will close the college, and it will reopen as Columbia.
suggested_refs: A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress (1774)
The Park Place campus of King's College, later Columbia

segments.name: The New York Company of Artillery

stops.name: Brooklyn Heights, the guns cover the retreat
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json so the two travelers share one pin on the Brooklyn lines.
stops.campa: Captain Hamilton of the New York Provincial Company of Artillery, twenty-one and commissioned on an examination in mathematics, brings his guns onto the Brooklyn lines as the army is flanked and broken on Long Island. George Washington takes the whole force off the island by night across the East River, in boats, in fog, without losing it. The British find the lines empty in the morning, and the campaign that follows is a retreat up the length of Manhattan.
suggested_refs: The Brooklyn Heights lines and the East River evacuation of 29-30 August 1776

stops.name: Harlem Heights, the disputed battery
stops.date_confidence: Tag dropped from attested to disputed. His presence is contested: Revolutionary War Journal finds no record of his artillery in the action and places his documented work in Putnam's retreat of 15 September, while other accounts do put his guns on the heights. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 40.8115, -73.9532 lands in the Harlem flats about a kilometre east of the battlefield and its monument.
stops.campa: On the heights above the Hollow Way an American advance turns and drives a British column back, the first thing resembling a victory in the New York campaign. Whether Hamilton's guns are on that ground is not settled. Some accounts put him there; others find no record of his company in the action and place his documented work in Israel Putnam's retreat up the island the day before. The atlas keeps both readings and picks neither. He is somewhere in those four miles with two field pieces.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Harlem Heights monument, near the Columbia campus
Revolutionary War Journal on the artillery at Harlem Heights
sources: Revolutionary War Journal, reported through the verification pass

stops.name: McConkey's Ferry, the guns over the ice
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json.
stops.campa: On Christmas night the army crosses the Delaware northward through drifting ice, and the artillery goes over on flat-bottomed Durham boats, horses and carriages and all, which takes longer than the men do and nearly costs the surprise. Hamilton has been sick and is thin and his company is down to a handful. Eighteen guns cross for two thousand four hundred men, a ratio no European army would recognize, because Washington has more cannon than trained infantry and means to use what he has.
suggested_refs: McConkey's Ferry crossing site, Delaware River, 25-26 December 1776

stops.name: Trenton, the head of King and Queen Streets
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json.
stops.campa: The guns are unlimbered at the head of King Street and Queen Street, firing down the two roads that run the length of the town, so that the Hessian regiments forming in the street have nowhere to form. The fight lasts under an hour. Colonel Rall is shot, nine hundred prisoners are taken, and a war that was ending in December is not ending. Hamilton's battery is doing the plainest work of his life, pointing metal down a street. The enlistments of most of the army expire in five days.
suggested_refs: The head of King and Queen Streets, Trenton, 26 December 1776

stops.name: Princeton, the shot at Nassau Hall
stops.date_confidence: The battle is attested; the cannonball is tradition, and Chernow doubts it. Coordinate: the pool's 40.3468, -74.6699 contradicted its own label, and since the claim carried is the Nassau Hall story rather than the battlefield action, this uses the Nassau Hall pin, inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json. Princeton Battlefield State Park lies at c. 40.3336, -74.6800.
stops.campa: Slipping around Cornwallis in the night, the army falls on the rear guard at Princeton, and British troops take shelter inside Nassau Hall. Tradition says a ball from Hamilton's battery goes through the wall and through a portrait of George the Second, and that the garrison comes out. Chernow doubts it, and the tradition is older than any document supporting it. The college that refused him admission four years earlier is the building he is said to have shot.
suggested_refs: Nassau Hall, Princeton, and the cannonball tradition
Princeton Battlefield State Park

stops.name: Morristown, aide-de-camp to the general
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the pool by six weeks. The pool gave 20 January 1777; Washington's General Orders of 1 March 1777 name the appointment, confirmed by Founders Online, Mount Vernon and the National Park Service.
stops.campa: Washington's general orders of the first of March name Alexander Hamilton aide-de-camp with the rank of lieutenant colonel. He has turned down two other generals for this. What the post means is writing: the commander's correspondence with Congress, with thirteen governors, with the French, in Washington's voice and over Washington's signature, at a volume no one man could dictate. For four years the letters that hold the Continental Army together are in his hand. He calls the staff the family and chafes inside it throughout.
suggested_refs: Washington's General Orders, 1 March 1777, Founders Online
The Morristown winter headquarters
sources: Library of Congress, Alexander Hamilton Papers timeline

stops.name: Valley Forge, the letters of a starving army
stops.date_confidence: The pool gives only winter 1777-1778. Month is set to the encampment and day defaults to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json.
stops.campa: Eleven thousand men encamp twenty miles from a Philadelphia the British are holding, and by February a quarter of them are dead or unfit. Hamilton writes the letters begging Congress and the states for flour, shoes and blankets that do not come, and drafts the answers to officers who think Horatio Gates should have the command instead. Lafayette is in the same camp, nineteen years old and paying for his own troops. Steuben arrives in the spring to drill an army Hamilton has spent the winter feeding on paper.
suggested_refs: The Valley Forge encampment, winter 1777-1778
Hamilton's supply correspondence for Washington, Founders Online

stops.name: Monmouth Court House, the horse shot under him
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the heat, on ground nobody has scouted, Charles Lee attacks the British rear guard and then withdraws, and the withdrawal becomes a rout coming back through the army marching up behind it. Hamilton rides into the retreating troops and rallies what he can; his horse is killed under him and he goes down with it. Washington rides up and relieves Lee on the field in front of everyone. Hamilton testifies at the court-martial that follows, and makes an enemy, which he does easily.
suggested_refs: The Monmouth battlefield and the Lee court-martial record

stops.name: Schuyler Mansion, Albany: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by the Library of Congress timeline and the Schuyler Mansion State Historic Site.
stops.campa: In the parlour of the Schuyler house above the Hudson, the illegitimate clerk from St. Croix marries Elizabeth Schuyler, second daughter of General Philip Schuyler, and enters by that door the Dutch patroon families who own the upper river. He has no money and no land, and the name is his father's without a marriage behind it; the family takes him anyway on the general's judgment. Elizabeth will outlive him by fifty years, spend them assembling his papers and denying what is said about him, and be buried at his feet.
suggested_refs: Schuyler Mansion State Historic Site, Albany
sources: Library of Congress, Alexander Hamilton Papers timeline

stops.name: Yorktown, Redoubt No. 10
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from marques_de_lafayette.journey.json and george_washington.journey.json so the three travelers share one pin. The HMDB marker for Redoubt 10 reads 37.2292, -76.4975; the discrepancy is recorded in the report and not resolved.
stops.campa: After a quarrel on a staircase he leaves Washington's staff and spends months asking for a field command, and gets one in time for the last siege. Lafayette gives him the order and he takes four hundred men against the seaward redoubt with unloaded muskets and fixed bayonets, so that nothing fires and gives them away. The work is carried in under ten minutes. The French take Redoubt Nine the same night, the siege lines close, and five days later Washington accepts Cornwallis's surrender on the same field.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Redoubts 9 and 10 on the Yorktown battlefield
Colonial National Historical Park tour stop D

stops.name: Albany, the first son and the bar
stops.date_confidence: Both events are attested to the year 1782 only, with no month in the pool, so month and day default to 01 and the two are given one stop rather than two on the same invented date.
stops.campa: In one year at Albany he becomes a father and a lawyer. Philip is born, the first of eight children. New York has suspended its clerkship requirement for men who served in the army, and Hamilton reads himself into the profession in a few months, writing as he goes a manual of practice that other students copy by hand for years afterward. He then takes as clients the loyalists whose property the state is confiscating, and argues in Rutgers against Waddington that a state law cannot override a treaty of the United States.
suggested_refs: Hamilton's manuscript Practical Proceedings in the Supreme Court of the State of New York
Rutgers v. Waddington (1784)
sources: Historical Society of the New York Courts, Alexander Hamilton

stops.name: New York City, the Bank of New York
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year 1784 in the pool with no month; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He writes the constitution of the Bank of New York and it opens for business in the Walton house, the first bank in the state and among the first in the country. There is no charter; the legislature will not grant one for seven years, so the thing operates on its own articles and its subscribers' nerve. He is twenty-nine. The articles he writes here are the draft he works from when he charters the Bank of the United States seven years later, and the bank itself is the oldest now operating in the country.
suggested_refs: The founding articles of the Bank of New York, 1784

stops.name: Maryland State House, Annapolis: the report that calls a convention
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json, which pins the same building for the 1783 resignation of his commission.
stops.campa: Twelve delegates from five states meet at Annapolis to discuss commercial regulation, which is far too few to decide anything, and Hamilton writes the report that turns the failure into an instrument. It asks the states to send delegates to Philadelphia the following May with a wider commission, to make the federal constitution adequate to the exigencies of the Union. Madison persuades him to soften the language before it goes out. The Constitutional Convention is called by the report of a meeting that failed.
suggested_refs: The Annapolis Convention report, September 1786
The Maryland State House, Annapolis

stops.name: Independence Hall, the six-hour speech
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The quote carried here is from his remarks of 26 June 1787, eight days later, and is dated in the quote source. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of June he rises and speaks for something near six hours, proposing a president and a senate serving during good behaviour, state governors appointed by the national government, and the British constitution named as the best model the world has produced. Nobody seconds it. He is outvoted two to one inside his own delegation by Yates and Lansing, who leave in July, and he goes home for stretches of the summer. The plan is remembered against him for the rest of his life and after it.
stops.quote: As long as offices are open to all men and no constitutional rank is established, it is pure republicanism.
stops.quote_source: Remarks in the Federal Convention, Philadelphia, 26 June 1787
suggested_refs: Madison's Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention, 18 and 26 June 1787
sources: Wikiquote, Alexander Hamilton, verified by direct fetch

stops.name: Independence Hall, the sole New York signature
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json. Note that a different William Paterson, of New Jersey, is in this room; he is not the William Paterson of the corpus, who founded the Bank of England.
stops.campa: He comes back for the signing and puts his name to a constitution containing almost nothing he proposed, alone for New York, since his two colleagues have gone home. Washington signs first as president of the convention. Benjamin Franklin, eighty-one, is helped forward, and says of the sun carved on the president's chair that he now knows it to be rising. Hamilton signs and begins at once the work of getting the document ratified, which will cost him more effort than writing one of his own.
suggested_refs: The engrossed Constitution and its signatures, National Archives
Madison's Notes, closing session, 17 September 1787

stops.name: New York City, Federalist No. 1
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day; published in the Independent Journal. Quote verified by direct fetch of the Avalon Project text.
stops.campa: The Independent Journal prints the first essay signed Publius, and over the next seven months eighty-five of them appear, at times four in a week. Hamilton writes more than half, John Jay falls ill after five, and Madison writes most of the rest, which is why the authorship of some twenty essays is still argued over and why no two editions agree. The pseudonym is a Roman who helped expel a king. The essays are newspaper polemic written to a deadline, and become the standard commentary on the document.
stops.quote: AFTER an unequivocal experience of the inefficiency of the subsisting federal government, you are called upon to deliberate on a new Constitution for the United States of America.
stops.quote_source: Federalist No. 1, Publius, Independent Journal, 27 October 1787 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)
suggested_refs: The Federalist, McLean edition, 1788
Avalon Project text of Federalist No. 1
sources: Library of Congress, Full Text of The Federalist Papers
Avalon Project, Yale Law School, verified by direct fetch

stops.name: New York City, Federalist No. 15
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. Quote verified by direct fetch of The Founders' Constitution, University of Chicago Press.
stops.campa: In the fifteenth essay he stops describing the Confederation and starts describing men. The argument is that a league of sovereign states asking for money it cannot compel is not a government at all, and that laws without a sanction are advice. He is writing from an office on Wall Street in the intervals of a law practice, in a state whose governor is against ratification and whose convention has not yet met. He is thirty-two and has never held an office higher than lieutenant colonel.
stops.quote: Why has government been instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not conform to the dictates of reason and justice, without constraint.
stops.quote_source: Federalist No. 15, Publius, 1 December 1787 (The Founders' Constitution, University of Chicago Press)
suggested_refs: Federalist No. 15 in The Founders' Constitution, vol. 1 ch. 5
sources: The Founders' Constitution, press-pubs.uchicago.edu, verified by direct fetch

stops.name: New York City, Federalist No. 78
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the McLean edition of 28 May 1788. The quote is corrected: the pool dropped two words from inside the second sentence without an ellipsis and compressed the first clause, and cited Wikiquote for a text the Avalon Project carries in full. Avalon is now the citation.
stops.campa: The seventy-eighth essay appears first in the bound McLean edition rather than in a newspaper, and it argues that judges holding office during good behaviour may set aside a statute contradicting the constitution, because the constitution is the people's act and the statute only the legislature's. Judicial review has no clause in the document itself; it has this essay. Fifteen years later John Marshall decides Marbury against Madison, and the reasoning is already in print, written to win a ratification vote.
stops.quote: The courts were designed to be an intermediate body between the people and the legislature... The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts.
stops.quote_source: Federalist No. 78, Publius, McLean edition, 28 May 1788 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)
suggested_refs: Avalon Project text of Federalist No. 78
Marbury v. Madison (1803)

stops.name: Poughkeepsie, the convention that ratifies by three votes
stops.date_confidence: Speech date attested. The quote is corrected and extended: the pool dropped the attributive phrase, which reversed the sense, printing an opponent's premise as Hamilton's own view. The full sentence and the sentence following it are carried, from the primary convention debates. Ratification follows on 26 July 1788.
stops.campa: New York's convention meets with an Antifederalist majority of roughly two to one under Governor George Clinton, and Hamilton argues against it for six weeks. He is not conceding the position he is usually quoted as holding; he states the other side's premise in order to break it. Virginia ratifies at the end of June and New Hampshire is the ninth state, so the Constitution will exist whatever Poughkeepsie decides, and the question becomes whether New York is inside it. On the twenty-sixth of July it ratifies, thirty to twenty-seven.
stops.quote: It has been observed by an honorable gentleman, that a pure democracy, if it were practicable, would be the most perfect government. Experience has proved, that no position in politics is more false than this.
stops.quote_source: First Speech of June 21, New York Ratifying Convention, Poughkeepsie, 21 June 1788 (Teaching American History, from the convention debates)
suggested_refs: The Dutchess County Courthouse site, Poughkeepsie
Debates of the New York Ratifying Convention, June-July 1788
sources: Teaching American History, First Speech of June 21
Historical Society of the New York Courts

stops.name: Federal Hall, the first Secretary of the Treasury
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: nominated and confirmed the same day. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json, which pins the same building for the first inaugural oath; the pool's 40.7072, -74.0102 differs by metres.
stops.campa: Washington sends the nomination to the Senate and the Senate confirms it the same day. The department Hamilton takes over has no money, no revenue system, and a war debt of some fifty-four million dollars owed at home and abroad, with the states owing twenty-five million more. He is thirty-four. Within two years he will employ more people than the rest of the federal government together, because the Treasury is the customs houses, the revenue cutters and the lighthouses, and the rest is a few clerks.
suggested_refs: Federal Hall National Memorial, Wall Street
The Senate executive journal, 11 September 1789
sources: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton (1789-1795)

stops.name: Federal Hall, the First Report on the Public Credit
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The quote is from a letter of 30 April 1781 to Robert Morris, nine years earlier, and is dated in the quote source; the fuller sentence about a powerful cement of union is widely circulated but was not confirmed against a primary fetch and is not carried.
stops.campa: The report goes to the House on the ninth of January and proposes that the federal government redeem the war debt at face value, in full, including the paper bought at a fraction of face by speculators from the soldiers paid in it, and that it assume the debts of the states as well. Madison moves to discriminate between original and current holders and is beaten. The argument is not about fairness. It is that a debt honoured without asking who holds it is the only thing that makes anyone lend again.
stops.quote: A national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing.
suggested_refs: First Report on the Public Credit, 9 January 1790
Hamilton to Robert Morris, 30 April 1781
sources: First Report on the Public Credit (1790)
Wikiquote, Alexander Hamilton, verified by direct fetch

stops.name: New York City, the bargain over dinner
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01. Jefferson's own account, written years later, is the principal source and is self-serving on the point of his own reluctance.
stops.campa: Assumption is dead in the House and the permanent capital is deadlocked between the Delaware and the Potomac, and Thomas Jefferson, newly back from Paris, has Hamilton and Madison to dinner. What comes out of the evening is that assumption passes and the capital goes south to a stretch of the Potomac after ten years in Philadelphia. Jefferson will write later that he was manipulated and regretted it more than any political act of his life. Nothing is written down that evening, and the account that survives is Jefferson's own, set down years afterward.
suggested_refs: Jefferson's account of the assumption dinner, in the Anas

stops.name: Philadelphia, the quarrel with Jefferson
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested for the Second Report on Public Credit and the removal of the government to Philadelphia; day defaults to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from thomas_jefferson.journey.json, which pins the same quarrel.
stops.campa: The government moves to Philadelphia and the Second Report on Public Credit asks for a national bank. Across the cabinet table Jefferson sees a bank, a funding scheme that enriches men who hold paper, and an admiration for the English constitution, and reads the three together as a monarchy assembling itself. Washington asks both of them, separately and in writing, to stop. Neither stops. Out of the quarrel between two of his secretaries come the first two political parties in the country.
stops.quote: a man whose history, from the moment at which history can stoop to notice him, is a tissue of machinations against the liberty of the country which has not only received and given him bread, but heaped it's honors on his head.
stops.quote_source: Thomas Jefferson to George Washington, 9 September 1792, on Hamilton
suggested_refs: The Jefferson and Hamilton cabinet papers, Founders Online
Second Report on Public Credit, December 1790

stops.name: Philadelphia, the bank chartered
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year 1791 in the pool with no month; month and day default to 01. The Philadelphia Treasury office address is a reconstruction: Chernow places the department near Independence Hall and the exact address is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Jefferson and Randolph tell Washington the bank is unconstitutional because no clause authorizes it. Hamilton answers in a week with the doctrine of implied powers: a government given ends is given the means, unless the means are forbidden. Washington signs. The First Bank of the United States opens with a fifth of its capital federal and the rest private, a design taken from the Bank of England that William Paterson had sold to a London government ninety-seven years earlier for the same reason, a state that needed to borrow.
suggested_refs: Hamilton's Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank, 23 February 1791
The First Bank of the United States building, Third Street, Philadelphia

stops.name: Philadelphia, Maria Reynolds and the hush money
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year 1791 in the pool with no month; month and day default to 01. The narrative of the first approach comes from Hamilton's own 1797 pamphlet and has no independent corroboration.
stops.campa: A young woman comes to his house saying her husband has abandoned her and she needs money to get back to New York. He brings it to her lodgings himself. The affair runs for months, and her husband James Reynolds learns of it and begins asking for payments, and Hamilton pays over a thousand dollars in instalments while continuing to run the finances of the United States. Reynolds is also speculating in exactly the veterans' claims the Treasury is redeeming, which is what makes the letters worth keeping.
suggested_refs: The Reynolds correspondence as printed in Hamilton's 1797 pamphlet
sources: Britannica, What was the Hamilton-Reynolds affair?

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Report on Manufactures
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day of submission. Quote verified by direct fetch of The Founders' Constitution text of the report.
stops.campa: The last of the great reports argues that the United States should not remain an agricultural exporter, and asks for protective tariffs, bounties for new industries, and public money for roads and canals. Adam Smith had published fifteen years earlier that such interference misallocates capital, and Hamilton has read him and answers him: a country without manufactures is a country dependent in war. Congress does not adopt it, and of the great reports it is the one that goes nowhere in his lifetime.
stops.quote: Women and Children are rendered more useful and the latter more early useful by manufacturing establishments... minds of the strongest and most active powers for their proper objects fall below mediocrity and labour without effect, if confined to uncongenial pursuits.
stops.quote_source: Report on the Subject of Manufactures, submitted to Congress 5 December 1791
suggested_refs: Report on the Subject of Manufactures (1791)
Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776)
sources: The Founders' Constitution, press-pubs.uchicago.edu, verified by direct fetch

stops.name: Bedford, the march against the whiskey counties
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01. The July climax at Bower Hill is attested but the pool supplies no coordinate for it, so the rebellion appears here only at the militia staging camp. The quote is from an essay of 28 August 1794 and is dated in the quote source.
stops.campa: The excise on distilled spirits falls hardest on farmers west of the mountains who move their grain as whiskey because they cannot move it as grain, and in July the resistance burns the excise inspector's house at Bower Hill and a man is killed. Washington federalizes thirteen thousand militia and rides out with them, the only sitting president to take the field. Hamilton goes too, and stays after Washington turns back, questioning prisoners. Twenty are taken to Philadelphia, two convicted, and both pardoned.
stops.quote: A sacred respect for the constitutional law is the vital principle, the sustaining energy of a free government.
stops.quote_source: Essay in the American Daily Advertiser, 28 August 1794
suggested_refs: The Bower Hill site, western Pennsylvania
The militia staging camp at Bedford, October 1794
sources: Mount Vernon, George Washington and the Whiskey Rebellion

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Farewell Address printed
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day of printing. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json; note that the interlock summary reported this pin as 39.9494, -75.15, and the file itself carries 39.9526, -75.1652, which is what is used. The resignation of 31 January 1795 is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: He resigned the Treasury in January of the previous year for money, the office paying three thousand a year against a growing family, and went back to a New York law practice. Washington sends him Madison's 1792 draft and asks for a valedictory. Hamilton writes most of what appears, on entangling alliances, on the danger of party, on the debt as a thing to be discharged rather than admired, and it is printed in a newspaper rather than spoken. Forty years later Andrew Jackson writes a farewell that answers it.
suggested_refs: The Farewell Address as printed in the American Daily Advertiser, 19 September 1796
Madison's 1792 draft and Hamilton's revision, Founders Online
sources: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton (1789-1795)

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Reynolds Pamphlet
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Accused in print of having used the Treasury to speculate through James Reynolds, he answers by publishing the whole affair, letters included, to prove the payments were blackmail over adultery and not corruption in office. Ninety-five pages. He is defending the only thing he thinks matters, which is that he never took public money, and he destroys in the process his marriage's privacy and any chance of the presidency. Elizabeth stays. His enemies reprint the pamphlet for years at their own expense.
suggested_refs: Observations on Certain Documents (the Reynolds Pamphlet), August 1797
sources: HISTORY.com, The Scandal That Ruined Alexander Hamilton's Chances of Becoming President

stops.name: The Capitol, the thirty-sixth ballot
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01. Geographic hedge: the pool places the episode at Washington, D.C., where the House balloted, and Hamilton's instrument was correspondence; the pool does not attest his presence in the chamber. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from andrew_jackson.journey.json, which pins the same building for the 1825 House election.
stops.campa: Jefferson and Aaron Burr tie in the electoral college and the House must choose, balloting by state, deadlocked through thirty-five rounds while Federalists consider putting in Burr to spite the Virginian. Hamilton writes to every Federalist he can reach urging Jefferson, whose principles he detests, over Burr, who he says has none. He is not in the chamber; his instrument is correspondence, as it has been since he was twenty-two. On the thirty-sixth ballot Jefferson is president, and Burr never forgives the letters.
suggested_refs: Hamilton's letters to Federalist congressmen, January-February 1801, Founders Online
sources: Constitution Center blog on the Burr-Hamilton feud

stops.name: New York City, the Evening Post
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Out of office and out of a national party, he raises about ten thousand dollars from Federalist merchants and founds the New-York Evening Post, installing William Coleman as editor and dictating leaders to him at night. The paper is a weapon against a Republican press that has beaten him, and it is the only institution he founds that is still publishing, under a shortened name, more than two centuries later. The first issue appears on the sixteenth of November 1801.
suggested_refs: The first issue of the New-York Evening Post, 16 November 1801

stops.name: Weehawken, Philip
stops.date_confidence: Dates attested: wounded 23 November, died 24 November 1801. The site is disputed and is not resolved here. Chernow and Wikipedia say Weehawken; Gilder Lehrman's Hamilton Education Program and PBS American Experience say Paulus Hook, present-day Jersey City, several miles away. The pool's claim that Philip died on the same ground as his father is unsupported and is dropped.
stops.campa: Philip Hamilton, nineteen, calls out a lawyer named George Eacker over a Fourth of July speech attacking his father, and is shot in the side and dies the next day. His father had advised him to fire in the air. Where it happened is disputed: Chernow says Weehawken, Gilder Lehrman and PBS say Paulus Hook across from the city, and both are named here without choosing. His sister Angelica loses her reason and does not recover. Hamilton is at the bedside, and the friends who see him in the months after describe a changed man.
suggested_refs: The Paulus Hook and Weehawken duelling grounds, both claimed for 23 November 1801

stops.name: Hamilton Grange, the thirteen sweetgums
stops.date_confidence: The pool gives the house as built 1800-1802 and occupied 1802-1804, with no month; month and day default to 01. Coordinate conflict within the pool is flagged: the geography lens gives 40.8214, -73.9472 and the afterlife lens 40.8236, -73.949 for the same estate, and the house itself has stood on three sites.
stops.campa: Nine miles north of the city he builds the only house he ever owns, a yellow federal-style villa on thirty-two acres of the Harlem heights, and names it the Grange after his father's people in Ayrshire. He plants thirteen sweetgum trees on the lawn for the thirteen states. He lives in it barely two years. The house is moved twice afterward, in 1889 to make way for the street grid and again in 2008 by hydraulic dolly into St. Nicholas Park, so that no coordinate on any map is where he built it.
suggested_refs: Hamilton Grange National Memorial, St. Nicholas Park
NPS, A Monumental Move, on the 2008 relocation

stops.name: New York City, the letter not to be delivered
stops.date_confidence: Date attested; the manuscript is headed only July 4. 1804 / Mrs. Hamilton, with no dateline. Place corrected: the pool put this letter at Weehawken, which is the duel ground of a week later. Hamilton was in New York City that day at the Society of the Cincinnati dinner.
stops.campa: A week before the meeting he writes his wife a letter to be opened only if he is dead, and dines the same evening with the Society of the Cincinnati, where Aaron Burr is also at the table and the two men are observed to be civil. He writes her a second letter on the tenth, and a statement of his reasons, in which he says he means to reserve his first fire. He writes about his own death three times in a week. To Burr he writes nothing, and the seconds settle the ground and the hour between them.
stops.quote: This letter, my very dear Eliza, will not be delivered to you, unless I shall first have terminated my earthly career.
suggested_refs: Hamilton's farewell letters to Elizabeth, 4 and 10 July 1804, Founders Online 01-26-02-0001-0248
sources: storyoftheweek.loa.org, The Duel: Once more Adieu, verified by direct fetch
Gilder Lehrman Institute, Hamilton's Farewell Letter to His Wife

stops.name: Weehawken, the ledge under the Palisades
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Coordinate corrected twice over: the geography lens gave 40.7645, -74.0134, about 800 m south-southeast and off the Palisades ledge, and the afterlife lens gave 40.7698, -74.0113, which at that latitude is in the Hudson. HMDB marker 7334 for the duelling ground at Hamilton Avenue and Boulevard East reads 40 deg 46.2 min N, 74 deg 1.032 min W. Whether Hamilton fired wide deliberately is disputed and is left open.
stops.campa: They are rowed across before seven in the morning to a ledge twenty feet above the river on the Jersey shore, where duelling is prosecuted less severely, and where his son may have died three years before. The seconds turn their backs so as to be able to swear they saw nothing. Two shots, close together. Hamilton's goes high into a tree limb above Burr's head; Burr's enters above the right hip, breaks a rib, tears the liver, and lodges in the spine. Whether Hamilton meant to miss is argued still.
stops.quote: I have resolved, if our interview is conducted in the usual manner... to reserve and throw away my first fire.
stops.quote_source: Hamilton's written statement of his reasons, the night before the duel, 10 July 1804
suggested_refs: The Weehawken duelling ground marker, HMDB 7334, Hamilton Avenue and Boulevard East
The Death Rock marker above the Hudson
sources: HISTORY.com, Aaron Burr slays Alexander Hamilton in duel
Library of Congress, A Tragic Duel

stops.name: Trinity Churchyard, the pyramid
stops.date_confidence: Burial date attested. The Bayard house on Jane Street, where he died on 12 July, is folded into this stop because the exact site is a reconstruction from period accounts, at c. 40.7359, -74.0075. The monument is not dated here: Trinity's Corporation put up a marker soon after the burial, but the surviving pyramid-topped marble is attributed to a later erection associated with the Society of the Cincinnati.
stops.campa: He is rowed back across the river and carried to William Bayard's house on Jane Street, where he lives thirty-one hours, receives communion after two clergymen have refused it to a duellist, and dies on the afternoon of the twelfth. The city closes for the funeral and the procession goes down to Trinity with his horse led behind the coffin, the boots reversed in the stirrups. Elizabeth outlives him by fifty years, dies in 1854, and is buried in the same churchyard.
stops.quote: the Patriot of Incorruptible Integrity, the Soldier of approved Valor, the Statesman of consummate Wisdom
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the Hamilton monument, Trinity Churchyard, New York

The William Bayard house site, Jane Street, Greenwich Village
sources: Trinity Church Wall Street parish records

stops.name: The Treasury, the face that stays on the note
stops.date_confidence: Corrected by ten months. The pool dated the reversal 18 June 2015, one day after the redesign announcement of 17 June 2015; in fact Lew announced the reversal on 20 April 2016, together with Tubman on the front of the twenty and the suffrage march on the ten's reverse. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from andrew_jackson.journey.json, which pins the same Treasury.
stops.campa: James Earl Fraser's bronze has stood on the south patio since 1923, ten feet of a man who never held elected office, outside the department he invented. In June 2015 a Treasury secretary announces that the ten-dollar note will be redesigned to carry a woman, and everyone assumes Hamilton goes. A musical drawn from Chernow's biography has just opened. On the twentieth of April 2016 the announcement is reversed: Hamilton stays, and Andrew Jackson is moved off the front of the twenty instead.
suggested_refs: James Earl Fraser's Hamilton bronze, Treasury south patio, dedicated 17 May 1923
The 20 April 2016 Treasury announcement on the ten and the twenty
